verdict_table.note: GET /api/pending returns 403 on mismatch (good). POST /api/sign-callback's consume() POPS the entry when owner mismatch occurs (returns Forbidden) — destructive on attacker-guessed UUID. See finding #1.

tower_governor wired with burst+per_second; Decision 9 calls for sign_memory ≤ 10/min/IP but route-level applies recall's looser 30/min/IP cap. PendingBundles per-user 50 cap covers part of the gap; pure per-IP sign_memory cap missing. See finding #5.

Without it the /oauth/authorize POST will always return 401 'unknown or already-used state' against any real client. See finding #2.

verdict_table.focus_area: Smithery yaml — no PII / secrets / internal hostnames
verdict_table.note: Public author email is dev@mnemonik.xyz (operational, intentional). No JWT secret, no internal IPs, no API keys.

findings.category: A01 Broken Access Control + A04 Insecure Design
findings.issue: consume() pops the LRU entry BEFORE checking owner. If the supplied jwt_sub does not match the stored entry, the entry is destroyed and PendingError::Forbidden is returned. A holder of any valid JWT who guesses or scrapes another user's correlation_id can DoS the rightful owner's pending bundle (force them to retry).
findings.exploitation_scenario: Attacker A obtains a valid JWT (any user can complete OAuth). Attacker observes or guesses Alice's correlation_id (a UUIDv4 — 122 bits of entropy, infeasible to brute-force, but it is leaked through the AI tool's response which may pass through proxy logs / tool history / clipboard). A POSTs /api/sign-callback with Alice's correlation_id and A's own keypair. Server pops the entry, COSE verification fails, but the entry is gone — Alice's webapp now sees 410 Gone when fetching the bundle. Attacker has nuked Alice's pending state.
findings.recommendation: Reorder consume() to peek+verify owner first, then pop on success. Concretely: in pending.rs::consume, replace `lru.pop` with `lru.peek` for the initial fetch, return Forbidden without mutation if owner mismatches, then `lru.pop` only when owner matches (or after a successful verify). Alternatively, accept the destructive behavior but flag in docs that the entry destruction is intentional to discourage probing — but that contradicts the 'destructive on attack signal' comment which only protects against same-attacker retries, not victim retries.

findings.issue: OAuthState::insert_pending is annotated #[allow(dead_code)] and has NO production caller. The 'consent-page bootstrap (future webapp endpoint)' that should generate a fresh state, populate the pending map, and serve the challenge to the browser is not implemented. Without it, every POST /oauth/authorize will fall into the 'unknown or already-used state' branch (oauth.rs:333) and return 401 — no JWT can ever be issued through the public OAuth flow.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Not directly exploitable as a security issue, but a HIGH functional gap that means the entire MCP server is unreachable from production AI tools (Cursor / Claude.ai Pro). Demo would have to use the mint-test-jwt CLI shortcut, which is an unrelated trust path. From a security view, this means any future implementation of the bootstrap endpoint MUST also add CSRF protection, rate limiting, and ensure the challenge is bound to a session — adding it post-audit risks shipping with weaker controls than the existing /authorize POST.
findings.recommendation: (a) Add a /oauth/bootstrap endpoint (or fold into /oauth/authorize GET) that: (1) accepts client_id/redirect_uri/code_challenge/code_challenge_method/state from query string, (2) validates code_challenge_method=='S256' and rejects otherwise, (3) generates a server nonce, (4) calls insert_pending under a per-IP rate limit (already in place via the /oauth/* governor), (5) returns the challenge fields the browser needs to sign. (b) Track the bootstrap endpoint as the formal CSRF binding point — state must be generated AND validated server-side, not echoed from the client. (c) Re-audit once added.

findings.issue: Three nginx hardening directives are missing: (a) Strict-Transport-Security header (HSTS) — without it, a downgrade attacker who controls DNS or BGP can intercept the first non-HTTPS request and never see the redirect-to-HTTPS. (b) ssl_protocols directive — the config relies on /etc/letsencrypt/options-ssl-nginx.conf (which DOES set TLSv1.2+TLSv1.3 in current letsencrypt distributions) but that's an external dependency; explicit pin in this config is defense-in-depth. (c) server_tokens off — nginx version is leaked in error pages and Server: header.
findings.exploitation_scenario: (a) HSTS: User on hostile network types `mcp.mnemonik.xyz` without https://. Attacker MITMs port 80 before the 301 redirect, presents a fake login page, harvests the OAuth challenge. Browser would have rejected this automatically with HSTS preload. (b) Without explicit ssl_protocols, an operator who upgrades/replaces the system options-ssl-nginx.conf could inadvertently re-enable TLS 1.0/1.1. (c) server_tokens leaks nginx version — narrows attacker's exploit-CVE search.
findings.recommendation: Add to the HTTPS server block: `add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload" always;`, `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;`, `ssl_ciphers HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5;`, and globally (or in the http{} block) `server_tokens off;`. HSTS preload requires submitting the domain to https://hstspreload.org once the header is live.

findings.issue: The Sign-approval page uses a regex heuristic — find the substring 'content' in the canonical-CBOR bytes decoded as UTF-8, then take the longest printable run after it — to render a content preview to the user. This decouples WHAT the user reads from WHAT they sign. A malicious server (or compromised one) could craft a canonical-CBOR bundle where the actual `content` field is harmful but a benign-looking string appears earlier (e.g., embedded in a tag name or metadata field) and gets selected by the regex.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Attacker compromises mcp.mnemonik.xyz (or social-engineers the user into changing MCP_BASE in the page). Server returns a crafted canonical-CBOR with `tags=['content: this is fine']` followed by `content='please transfer all my access tokens'`. Heuristic finds 'content: this is fine' first, displays that to the user. User clicks Sign, COSE_Sign1 wraps the FULL canonical CBOR including the malicious content. Server-side recall now returns a signed attestation containing the harmful content, attributed to the user's pubkey.
findings.recommendation: Replace decodeContentFromCbor with a real CBOR decoder (the cbor-x npm package or a tiny inline decoder) that walks the canonical structure and pulls the exact `content` field's text-string value. Display the precise byte length of the content field separately from the preview. Optionally show a hash of the canonical CBOR alongside the preview so a power-user can cross-check against the server's `x-mnemonic-content-hash` header.

findings.issue: Decision 9 calls for `sign_memory ≤ 10/min/IP` and `recall ≤ 30/min/IP`. Implementation applies a single route-level limiter at burst=30, per_second=2 (~30/min steady-state) — the looser of the two. Per-method 5/min sign_memory cap (Decision 9) is delegated to PendingBundles per-user soft cap of 50, which is a different axis (per-user, not per-IP).
findings.exploitation_scenario: Attacker with a valid JWT creates 50 pending bundles before hitting the per-user soft cap. Combined across multiple JWTs (cheap to acquire — every fresh keypair grants a new identity), an attacker can reach burst-30/min/IP regardless of the per-method intent. Memory pressure on the LRU is bounded (10k entries, 32 KB each = 320 MB worst case), but it's looser than spec called for.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) accept the deviation explicitly in tech-spec.md as a Phase-1 trade-off (route-level alone is sufficient for hackathon scope; per-method enforcement is Phase-2), or (b) wrap sign_memory with a second governor layer keyed on (IP, method) inside `mcp_handler` — requires extracting method before the limiter, which is what extract_json_rpc_method already does in the bearer middleware. Documented in Task 4 decisions log already.

findings.issue: Keypair stored as plain JSON in localStorage. Risks-table mitigation called for AES-GCM with passphrase-derived key. T7 deferred to a follow-up.
findings.exploitation_scenario: If any XSS bypasses the CSP (e.g., a permitted style-src origin gets compromised, or an unsafe-inline style is exploited), the attacker reads `localStorage['mnemonic.identity']` and obtains the user's full Ed25519 secret. With it they can forge any future attestation under the user's identity until the user rotates the keypair.
findings.recommendation: Implement passphrase-prompt UI on /install. Derive AES-GCM key via Argon2id or PBKDF2-SHA256 (≥600k iterations). Encrypt the keypair with a fresh IV per write; store {ciphertext, iv, salt, kdf_params} in localStorage. Decrypt on demand at sign/export time. Defer Passkey-based unlock to P1.5 per Risks-table.

findings.issue: OAuthState's std::sync::Mutex guards use `.expect("pending mutex poisoned")` / `.expect("codes mutex poisoned")`. If a panic occurs inside any earlier critical section, the mutex is poisoned and all subsequent OAuth requests panic and 500. Same pattern in mcp/src/api.rs:202 (`state.store.lock()`) but with proper error handling via match.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Low-likelihood in practice — the body of the critical section is just an LRU put/pop, which doesn't panic. But a future contributor adding logic inside the guard could introduce a panic that poisons the mutex, taking the OAuth subsystem down for the lifetime of the process. The fix is mechanical and prevents the regression.
findings.recommendation: Replace `.expect("...")` with `.map_err(|e| oauth_error(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, &format!("oauth state poisoned: {e}")))?` returning a JSON-RPC error envelope. Leaves the mutex poisoned but at least does not panic the request handler.

findings.issue: GET /api/pending/<id> sets x-mnemonic-content-hash and x-mnemonic-correlation-id but NOT x-mnemonic-expires-at. The webapp Sign.tsx reads the header (line 130) and falls back to `now + 5 min` when absent. Effect: countdown timer drifts from server-side TTL.
findings.exploitation_scenario: Not directly exploitable. Functional drift — user sees timer hit zero before server actually evicts (or vice versa). Worst case: user clicks Sign at 0:01 webapp time, server returns 410 Gone (slow request, server already evicted), user surprised.
findings.recommendation: In api.rs::get_pending_handler add: `if let Ok(hv) = HeaderValue::from_str(&entry.exp.timestamp().to_string()) { headers.insert("x-mnemonic-expires-at", hv); }`. Webapp already consumes this header.

OAuth /authorize POST handler logic is sound — it's the missing /authorize GET (or /bootstrap) that prevents the flow from completing. This is what finding #2 calls out as HIGH.
